newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-Australian Broadcasting Corp Morning Update.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-Australian Broadcasting Corp Morning Update.

text.p: NEW SA LEADER TO BE SWORN IN
South Australia's new Premier will be officially sworn in this morning.
John Olsen will take over from Dean Brown, who stood aside after the Liberal Party room voted for a spill last night.
Mr Brown will move to the backbench and says he's yet to decide if he wants to be a minister.
Graham Ingerson is the new Deputy Premier, after defeating Stephen Baker, 24 votes to 10.
FRINGE BENEFITS TAX MAY CHANGE
Deputy Prime Minister Tim Fischer says the mining industry has a right to argue the Government should eliminate further anomolies in the Fringe Benefits Tax.
Mr Fischer says he welcomes submissions the industry has recently made, but more may be needed to demonstrate the impact FBT is having on things such as fly-in fly-out mining operations.
He says mining companies can take heart from the recent abolition of the tax relating to pastoral accommodation in remote areas.
Mr Fischer was speaking in the Western Australian mining heartland of Kalgoorlie.
GOVT TAKES POSSESSION OF LOCOS
Prime Minister John Howard and Federal Transport Minister John Sharp will today take delivery of two locomotives in Newcastle as part of a 420 million dollar National Rail Corporation contract.
The contract was won by Broadmeadow train builder Goninan last September and has created hundreds of new jobs.
National Rail's order for 120 locomotives is Australia's largest ever diesel electric locomotive contract.
The Prime Minister and the Transport Minister will accept delivery of the two locomotives this morning.
AMBASSADOR SAYS AUSTRALIANS HAVE WRONG VIEW OF INDONESIA
The Indonesian Ambassador says he's concerned a large proportion of Australians still see Indonesia as a security threat.
Ambassador Sastrohandojo Wirjono told an Internationalising Communities Conference in Toowoomba, Australia's trade relations with Indonesia are excellent.
Mr Wirjono says he's confident the 1996 Security Agreement between the countries will build trust and allay suspicions.
SEVEN NETWORK STAFF MEET OVER DISPUTE
Seven Network employees around Australia meet again this morning to decide whether to continue industrial action over a redundancy deal.
The action has forced the network to abandon coverage today of the Greg Norman Golf Classic, and has affected news coverage and filming of drama.
The stoppage began yesterday after executives rejected a deal negotiated earlier this week on a redundancy package for 119 workers losing their jobs.
RABBIT VIRUS RESULTS ENCOURAGING
Primary Industries Minister, John Anderson, says there are encouraging signs from the first monitoring of the spread of the rabbit calici virus across Australia.
The virus has been officially released at 181 sites across mainland Australia in the past two months.
Mr Anderson says reports indicate the virus has already significantly improved the chances of the long-term sustainability of millions of hectares of rabbit-prone country.
He says data shows wild rabbit populations are being reduced by between 80 and 95 per cent within eight weeks of the virus's release.
CLAIMS DEATH LAW MAY HAVE COME TOO QUICKLY
An expert on caring for the dying says the Northern Territory has been too quick to legalise euthanasia.
Terry Altilio specialises in providing care to patients in pain at New York's Memorial Sloan-Kettering Cancer Centre.
She was speaking in Brisbane at the 23rd annual meeting of the Oncological Society of Australia.
Ms Altilio has questioned whether the Territory Government fully investigated caring for the dying before adopting the controversial euthanasia law.
OFFENSIVE MUSIC BLAMED FOR SUICIDES
It's claimed songs with offensive lyrics are encouraging young people to kill themselves.
New South Wales State MP Grant McBride is calling for a ban on CDs with offensive lyrics, including a band call Suicidal Tendancies.
He's asking the Prime Minister to ban such music being played on the electronic media.
Mr McBride says at a recent Suicide Summit, many parents whose children had committed suicide, felt they had been influenced to take their lives by certain types of music.
-- Reuters Sydney Newsroom 61-2 9373-1800
